Philosophy.Principle: Comments exist to explain WHY, never WHAT. Self-documenting code — achieved through clear naming and structure — is the primary documentation mechanism. A comment that restates what the code already expresses is noise that degrades maintainability.

Four mechanisms govern clear code communication in this order of preference: (1) naming, (2) structure, (3) context, (4) comments. Reach for a comment only when the first three cannot carry the intent.

Comments provide the most value when they expose non-intuitive behaviour: edge-case workarounds, performance trade-offs, historical context, and complex business rules not obvious from the code structure.

Self-documenting code is championed by Robert C. Martin ("Uncle Bob"), Google's engineering style guides, and Python's PEP 8. When code is expressive enough, remaining comments can focus exclusively on the reasoning behind decisions.

Prefixing a comment with a structured label makes intention immediately clear, changes tone deliberately, prompts actionable follow-up, encourages collaboration, and — critically — makes comments machine-parseable for tooling.

[NEW in v3.0] Code is now read by two audiences: human developers AND AI coding agents. Structured labels serve both. Prefer semantic density: every comment token must earn its place. An ETH Zurich study (AGENTbench, 2026) confirms that human-curated, semantically precise annotations outperform verbose LLM-generated context files in agent task success rates.

[NEW in v3.0] When an AI coding agent edits a file, the comments it encounters form part of its operational context. Labels such as Contract:, Invariant:, and Assume: are therefore not just for human readers — they constrain and guide agent behaviour directly. Write them with both audiences in mind.

FormattingConventions.Rule: Place comments on their own line — never trailing a code statement, except for inline data literals (see F6).
Begin comment text with a capitalised word, treating it as a sentence.
Keep each line under 100 characters. (80 for legacy codebases; 100 is the modern default per Google and Airbnb style guides.)
Insert exactly one space between the delimiter (//, #, --) and the label.
Align the comment with the indentation of the code block it describes.
For inline data literals (colour arrays, magic numbers, enums), inline alignment of trailing comments IS acceptable when it dramatically improves readability — e.g. RGB tuples.
Write code comments in English by default. Exceptions apply only when the entire team shares another language and the code will never be read externally.
One label, one action. Never join two actions with "and".

[NEW in v3.0] For agent-targeted annotations (CAT-10), always use a structured key-value form inside the comment body so that parsers and LLMs can extract them reliably. Example: // Contract: pre=x>0, post=result>0, throws=ArgumentException
[NEW in v3.0] Use imperative-mood verbs, not nouns or passive voice. "Filter expired items" not "Expired item filtering" or "Expired items are filtered here".

LabelDecisionTree.Question: Is this comment documenting a PUBLIC API surface?
LabelDecisionTree.AnswerYes: → Use DocCommentStandards (TSDoc / XML-doc / Google Docstring). Do not use inline labels.
LabelDecisionTree.Question: Is this a time-sensitive or work-in-progress marker?
LabelDecisionTree.AnswerYes: → Use a TemporalMarker (TODO, FIXME, HACK, TEMP, DEADLINE, DEPRECATED, BREAKING).
LabelDecisionTree.Question: Is this comment primarily for an AI/coding-agent consumer?
LabelDecisionTree.AnswerYes: → Use CAT-10 Agent Annotation labels (Contract, Invariant, Assume, AgentHint, AgentSkip, Boundary).
LabelDecisionTree.Question: Does the comment describe validation / checking?
Does the comment describe creating, mutating, or deleting an object?
LabelDecisionTree.AnswerYes: → CAT-2 (Create, Assign, Update, Add, Remove, Clone, Merge, Initialize).
LabelDecisionTree.Question: Does the comment describe a computation, transformation, or aggregation?
LabelDecisionTree.AnswerYes: → CAT-3 (Compute, Transform, Parse, Format, Filter, Generate, Normalize, Aggregate, Sort, Explain).
LabelDecisionTree.Question: Does the comment describe a domain event, business rule, or policy?
LabelDecisionTree.AnswerYes: → CAT-4 (Enforce, Raise, Trigger, Notify, Handle, Subscribe).
LabelDecisionTree.Question: Does the comment describe async flow, retries, batching, or rate control?
LabelDecisionTree.AnswerYes: → CAT-5 (Await, Retry, Skip, Fallback, Batch, Throttle, Defer, Continue, Break).
LabelDecisionTree.Question: Does the comment describe resource acquisition, caching, or cleanup?
LabelDecisionTree.AnswerYes: → CAT-6 (Acquire, Release, Lock, Cache, Purge, Pool, Dispose).
LabelDecisionTree.Question: Does the comment describe exception handling, degradation, or rollback?
LabelDecisionTree.AnswerYes: → CAT-7 (Catch, Recover, Compensate, Degrade, Escalate, Suppress).
LabelDecisionTree.Question: Does the comment describe an external integration boundary?
LabelDecisionTree.AnswerYes: → CAT-8 (Call, Send, Receive, Publish, Map, Serialize, Deserialize, Webhook).
LabelDecisionTree.Question: Does the comment describe logging, tracing, metrics, or audit?
LabelDecisionTree.AnswerYes: → CAT-9 (Log, Trace, Monitor, Audit, Profile, Debug).
LabelDecisionTree.AnswerNo: → Consider whether a comment is necessary. If it is, use the closest matching label and add a team-vocab extension.

Category.name: Validation and Checks
Category.Description: Preconditions, input validation, and conditional assertions. Use liberally around business-rule enforcement. Security-sensitive: always name the threat being mitigated.

Label.name: Validate:
Label.When: Input or data must meet a format or business-rule requirement.

Label.name: Check:
Label.When: Assert a condition before proceeding — null checks, existence, permissions.

Label.name: Guard:
Label.When: Defensive boundary check to prevent runtime errors. Name the threat (null, overflow, injection).

Label.name: Verify:
Label.When: Confirm post-condition or system state after an operation.
Label.Example: // Verify: Transaction committed successfully before releasing lock Debug.Assert(transaction.Status == TransactionStatus.Committed);

Label.name: Assert:
Label.When: Development-time invariant that must never be false; stripped or silent in production builds.
Label.Example: // Assert: All order items carry a positive price Debug.Assert(order.Items.All(i => i.Price > 0));

AntiPattern.Good: // Check: Order total exceeds zero before payment gateway call
AntiPattern.Reason: Labels must narrow intent, not echo the label word itself.

Category.name: Object Operations
Category.Description: Object lifecycle — creation, mutation, deletion, and merging.

Label.name: Create:
Label.When: Instantiate a new domain object or value type.
Label.Example: // Create: Order entity with default pending status var order = Order.Create(customerId);

Label.name: Assign:
Label.When: Set a property value; include the business reason, not the mechanics.
Label.Example: // Assign: Priority based on customer tier — premium orders fulfil first order.Priority = customer.Tier == Tier.Premium ? Priority.High : Priority.Normal;

Label.name: Update:
Label.When: Modify an existing object's state.
Label.Example: // Update: Shipping address from latest customer profile order.ShippingAddress = customer.PrimaryAddress;

Label.name: Add:
Label.When: Insert an element into a collection.

Label.name: Remove:
Label.When: Delete from a collection or mark for soft-delete.
Label.Example: // Remove: Expired items from cart before checkout to prevent stale pricing cart.Items.RemoveAll(item => item.ExpiresAt < DateTime.UtcNow);

Label.name: Clone:
Label.When: Produce an independent copy — deep or shallow — of an object. Specify depth.
Label.Example: // Clone: User preferences as deep copy for rollback snapshot var backupPrefs = user.Preferences.DeepClone();

Label.name: Merge:
Label.When: Combine data from multiple sources with defined conflict resolution.
Label.Example: // Merge: CRM and account data, account wins on conflict var customer = CustomerMerger.Merge(crmData, accountData, prioritizeAccount: true);

Label.name: Initialize:
Label.When: Populate defaults or calculated values during object setup.
Label.Example: // Initialize: Cart with customer's preferred currency and primary address cart.Initialize(customer.PreferredCurrency, customer.ShippingAddress);

Label.name: Reset:
Label.When: [NEW in v3.0] Return an object to a known default state without full re-creation.
Label.Example: // Reset: Form state to pristine after successful submission form.reset(DEFAULT_FORM_VALUES);

Category.name: Processing Logic
Category.Description: Computations, data transformations, aggregations, and formatting. Use verbs rather than nouns (TDS Jan 2025).

Label.name: Compute:
Label.When: Derive a calculated value — totals, scores, rates. State the formula or algorithm.
Label.Example: // Compute: Order total inclusive of regional tax rate (subtotal × (1 + taxRate)) order.Total = order.Subtotal * (1 + taxRate);

Label.name: Transform:
Label.When: Convert an object from one representation to another. Name both sides.
Label.Example: // Transform: CustomerDto → Customer domain entity via AutoMapper profile var customer = _mapper.Map<Customer>(customerDto);

Label.name: Parse:
Label.When: Extract structured data from raw text, bytes, or environment input.
Label.Example: // Parse: Feature-flag configuration from APP_CONFIG env var (JSON format) var config = ConfigParser.Parse(Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable("APP_CONFIG"));

Label.name: Format:
Label.When: Structure data for display, serialisation, or logging output.

Label.name: Filter:
Label.When: Remove unwanted elements from a collection based on a predicate.
Label.Example: // Filter: Active subscriptions only — excludes cancelled and trial-expired var active = subscriptions.Where(s => s.IsActive).ToList();

Label.name: Generate:
Label.When: Produce derived data — IDs, hashes, tokens, reference codes.

Label.name: Normalize:
Label.When: Standardise format or encoding — phone numbers, currencies, casing.
Label.Example: // Normalize: Phone to E.164 format for SMS gateway compatibility var phone = PhoneUtil.FormatE164(customer.Phone, customer.Country);

Label.name: Aggregate:
Label.When: Combine multiple values into a summary metric or projection.

Label.name: Sort:
Label.When: Order data by a business-meaningful criterion — not just alphabetically. State the criterion.

Label.name: Explain:
Label.When: [NEW in v3.0] Describe the algorithmic or mathematical reasoning behind a non-obvious implementation choice. Use for O(n²) trade-offs, domain formulas, or counter-intuitive optimisations.

Category.name: Events and Business Rules
Category.Description: Domain events, policy enforcement, and workflow triggers. The distinction between Raise (internal domain event) and Trigger (external workflow) is intentional.

Label.name: Enforce:
Label.When: Apply a business invariant or policy that must not be violated.

Label.name: Raise:
Label.When: Emit an internal domain event for the current aggregate.
Label.Example: // Raise: InventoryReservedEvent so warehouse handler picks up line items order.RaiseEvent(new InventoryReservedEvent(order.Items));

Label.name: Trigger:
Label.When: Initiate an external workflow, saga, or background process.
Label.Example: // Trigger: Email verification workflow for new registrant await _workflows.TriggerAsync(WorkflowType.EmailVerification, user.Id);

Label.name: Notify:
Label.When: Dispatch a notification to users, admins, or external systems.
Label.Example: // Notify: Security team of anomalous login pattern via PagerDuty webhook await _alerts.NotifySecurityAsync($"Unusual login from {ipAddress} for {user.Email}");

Label.name: Handle:
Label.When: Process an inbound domain or integration event inside a handler.

Label.name: Subscribe:
Label.When: Register a listener for domain or integration events.

Label.name: Policy:
Label.When: [NEW in v3.0] Reference a named business or compliance policy that governs the block. Enables grep-based policy audits.
Label.Example: // Policy: GDPR Article 17 — right to erasure; anonymise, do not delete customer.Anonymize();

Category.name: Flow Control and Coordination
Category.Description: Async operations, retry policies, short-circuits, and batching. Essential for async-heavy microservice codebases.

Label.name: Await:
Label.When: Wait on an async operation; document timeout or cancellation semantics.
Label.Example: // Await: External payment API — 30 s timeout, CancellationToken from caller var response = await _httpClient.PostAsync(endpoint, payload, cts.Token);

Label.name: Retry:
Label.When: Re-attempt after a transient failure with a defined policy.
Label.Example: // Retry: DB query on transient SQL exception — exponential backoff, max 3 attempts var result = await _retryPolicy.ExecuteAsync(() => _db.QueryAsync(sql, parameters));

Label.name: Skip:
Label.When: Bypass a code path under a well-defined condition. State the condition explicitly.

Label.name: Fallback:
Label.When: Use an alternative data source or strategy when the primary fails.
Label.Example: // Fallback: Serve cached pricing if catalogue service unavailable (stale < 15 min) var prices = await _catalogue.GetPricesAsync() ?? _cache.GetPrices();

Label.name: Batch:
Label.When: Group multiple operations for efficiency or rate compliance.

Label.name: Throttle:
Label.When: Limit operation rate to avoid overloading downstream services. State the limit.

Label.name: Defer:
Label.When: Postpone an operation for later execution — queue, scheduler, or hook.

Label.name: Continue:
Label.When: Explicitly proceed to the next loop iteration for readability.

Label.name: Break:
Label.When: Exit a loop or pipeline early on a well-defined condition.

Label.name: Circuit:
Label.When: [NEW in v3.0] Open a circuit breaker or reference an existing one. Name the threshold and the state (open/half-open/closed).
Label.Example: // Circuit: Open after 5 consecutive failures — 30 s recovery window await _circuitBreaker.ExecuteAsync(() => _service.CallAsync(request));

Category.name: Resource Management
Category.Description: Connections, locks, cache entries, and cleanup. Critical for preventing leaks in long-running services.

Label.name: Acquire:
Label.When: Obtain a scarce resource — connection, lock, file handle, semaphore.

Label.name: Release:
Label.When: Explicitly free a resource outside of a using/try-finally scope.

Label.name: Lock:
Label.When: Establish exclusive access to a shared in-process resource.
Label.Example: // Lock: Synchronise access to shared metrics accumulator (not Interlocked — complex update) lock (_metricsSync) { _metrics.OrderCount++; }

Label.name: Cache:
Label.When: Store a computed or fetched value for subsequent fast retrieval. State TTL and invalidation strategy.
Label.Example: // Cache: Exchange rates valid 15 min — FX API rate-limit is 100 calls/h _cache.Set(cacheKey, rates, TimeSpan.FromMinutes(15));

Label.name: Purge:
Label.When: Remove stale, expired, or invalid entries from a cache or store.
Label.Example: // Purge: Session tokens older than 24 h from Redis to comply with session policy await _sessionStore.PurgeExpiredAsync(olderThan: TimeSpan.FromHours(24));

Label.name: Pool:
Label.When: Borrow or return an instance from a managed resource pool.
Label.Example: // Pool: Borrow HTTP client pre-configured for payment-gateway mTLS var client = _httpPool.Get("payment-gateway");

Label.name: Dispose:
Label.When: Explicitly release managed and unmanaged resources at end of scope.

Category.name: Error Handling and Recovery
Category.Description: Exception handling, graceful degradation, and rollback. Label catch blocks individually — one label per exception type.

Label.name: Catch:
Label.When: Handle a specific, named exception type with intention.

Label.name: Recover:
Label.When: Attempt to restore a valid system state after an error.

Label.name: Compensate:
Label.When: Roll back side-effects of a failed operation (saga compensation).
Label.Example: // Compensate: Release reserved inventory on payment failure (saga step 3 rollback) await _inventory.ReleaseReservationAsync(order.Items);

Label.name: Degrade:
Label.When: Reduce to a safe subset of functionality while core features continue.
Label.Example: // Degrade: Route to manual processing queue — avoids order loss during outage await _manualQueue.EnqueueAsync(order.Id);

Label.name: Escalate:
Label.When: Re-throw or forward an error to a higher-level handler.
Label.Example: // Escalate: Unrecoverable payment failure — surface to API layer for 500 response throw new OrderProcessingException("Payment failed", ex);

Label.name: Suppress:
Label.When: Intentionally swallow a non-critical exception. ALWAYS document WHY suppression is safe here.
Label.Example: // Suppress: Optional telemetry failure must not block order flow (best-effort only) catch (TelemetryException) { /* intentionally empty */ }

Category.name: Integration and Communication
Category.Description: External API calls, message publishing, and data mapping. Always include system name and contract version where possible.

Label.name: Call:
Label.When: Invoke an external service or internal remote procedure. Name the system and contract version.
Label.Example: // Call: Identity provider (Okta) v2 API to validate bearer token var identity = await _idp.ValidateTokenAsync(bearerToken);

Label.name: Send:
Label.When: Transmit a command or document to an external system.
Label.Example: // Send: Confirmed order to warehouse fulfilment API (FulfilmentDto v3) await _warehouse.SendOrderAsync(fulfilmentDto);

Label.name: Receive:
Label.When: Ingest data arriving from an external source.

Label.name: Publish:
Label.When: Broadcast an event onto a message bus for fan-out consumers.
Label.Example: // Publish: OrderStatusChangedEvent — consumed by notifications and analytics await _bus.PublishAsync(new OrderStatusChangedEvent(order.Id, newStatus));

Label.name: Map:
Label.When: Convert between different data models at a boundary layer.
Label.Example: // Map: Domain order → OrderResponse DTO (wire format for v2 API consumers) var response = _mapper.Map<OrderResponse>(order);

Label.name: Serialize:
Label.When: Convert an object to a transmittable or storable format. State the target format.

Label.name: Deserialize:
Label.When: Reconstruct a typed object from raw transmitted data. State the source format.

Label.name: Webhook:
Label.When: Handle and validate an inbound webhook request.

Category.name: Observability and Debugging
Category.Description: Logging, distributed tracing, metrics, and compliance audit. Favour structured logging (key-value pairs) over string interpolation.

Label.name: Log:
Label.When: Record a business event or diagnostic fact for troubleshooting.

Label.name: Trace:
Label.When: Open a distributed trace span for cross-service correlation.

Label.name: Monitor:
Label.When: Emit a metric counter, gauge, or histogram for dashboards.

Label.name: Audit:
Label.When: Record a tamper-evident entry for compliance or security review.

Label.name: Profile:
Label.When: Bracket a performance-sensitive section for measurement.

Label.name: Debug:
Label.When: Temporary diagnostic output — MUST be removed before merging to main. Use the TEMP temporal marker alongside this label.
Label.Example: # TEMP Debug: Dump raw payload to verify upstream schema change — remove before merge print(f"[DEBUG] raw_payload={payload!r}")

Category.name: AI and Agent Annotations
Category.Description:
[NEW in v3.0] Structured annotations consumed by AI coding agents, static analysers, and formal verification tools. Based on the Semantic Density Principle (arXiv:2604.07502) and Design-by-Contract conventions.
Use a KEY=VALUE form so parsers can extract values without natural-language interpretation. These labels sit between doc-comments (CAT-API contracts) and inline labels (CAT-1 to CAT-9) in terms of formality.
KEY INSIGHT: An ETH Zurich AGENTbench study (2026) found that human-curated, tightly scoped annotations outperform verbose AI-generated context files. Every token in a CAT-10 comment must earn its place.

Label.name: Contract:
Label.When: Specify a formal pre/post-condition and exception contract for a function. Use at function entry. Enables Design-by-Contract tooling and agent reasoning.
Label.Example: # Contract: pre=len(items)>0, post=sum(result)==sum(items), throws=ValueError def normalize_weights(items: list[float]) -> list[float]: ...

Label.name: Invariant:
Label.When: Declare a property that must always be true for a class or data structure. Place at class or struct level. Agents must not violate these.
Label.Example: // Invariant: Total >= 0; Status is never null; Items.Count >= 1 when Status == Placed public class Order { }

Label.name: Assume:
Label.When: Document an assumption the code makes that is NOT enforced with a guard. Forces the agent to surface the assumption rather than silently rely on it.
Label.Format: // Assume: CONDITION — REASON why enforcement is omitted
Label.Example: # Assume: input_df has no NaN values — caller guarantees upstream cleaning pipeline def compute_percentiles(input_df: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.Series: ...

Label.name: AgentHint:
Label.When: Provide explicit guidance to AI coding agents on how to edit or extend this block. Use when the intent is non-obvious and auto-completion patterns would otherwise produce incorrect modifications.

Label.name: AgentSkip:
Label.When: Mark a block that AI agents MUST NOT auto-refactor or rewrite. Use for hand-tuned algorithms, legal text, compliance-critical code, or code where the LLM context window would lose essential nuance.
Label.Example: // AgentSkip: Hand-tuned SIMD vectorisation; auto-refactoring breaks alignment guarantees unsafe void ProcessBatchSIMD(float* src, float* dst, int length) { }

Label.name: Boundary:
Label.When: Mark an architectural boundary that agents must respect. Prevents agents from introducing cross-layer dependencies or leaking abstractions.
Label.Example: // Boundary: Domain → Infrastructure — do not import EF Core types above this line public interface IOrderRepository { }

Label.name: Context:
Label.When: Supply background context that is NOT in the code itself but is needed for correct interpretation — links to ADRs, tickets, external specs.

TemporalMarkers.Description: Temporal markers prefix inline labels to surface time-sensitive context. Format: MARKER(owner, ISO-date): reason — ticket reference IDEs such as IntelliJ IDEA and VS Code aggregate these automatically.

Marker.name: TODO
Marker.Format: // TODO(jane.smith, 2026-06-01): Replace with PaymentService v2 — TICKET-1234
Marker.When: Planned work not yet complete. Include owner and deadline.

Marker.name: FIXME
Marker.Format: // FIXME(ops-team, 2026-04-15): Memory leak on scroll listener — TICKET-5678
Marker.When: Known defect that needs correction before the next release.

Marker.name: HACK
Marker.Format: // HACK(platform, 2026-03-01): Workaround for rate-limit bug in SDK v3.1 — TICKET-9999
Marker.When: Temporary or suboptimal workaround that must be revisited.

Marker.name: TEMP
Marker.Format: // TEMP: Debug logging active — remove before merge
Marker.When: Short-lived code added for a specific investigation or deploy window.

Marker.name: DEADLINE
Marker.Format: // DEADLINE(2026-06-15): Remove feature flag after full rollout — TICKET-9012
Marker.When: Hard expiry date attached to a code path or feature toggle.

Marker.name: DEPRECATED
Marker.When: Mark an API or method scheduled for removal. Align with @deprecated doc-comment tags (JSDoc / TSDoc / C# XML-doc).

Marker.name: BREAKING
Marker.Format: // BREAKING(2026-07-01): Return type changes from string to UUID — bump major semver
Marker.When: [NEW in v3.0] Flag a change that breaks backward compatibility. Essential for library authors and API publishers.

Marker.name: PERF
Marker.Format: // PERF(john.doe, 2026-05-01): Profiled at 340 ms P99 — optimise before GA — TICKET-2345
Marker.When: [NEW in v3.0] Flag a performance bottleneck with measured data. Include the measurement and target.

ConventionalCommentsExtension.Description: For code-review comments the Conventional Comments standard (conventionalcomments.org) adds decoration qualifiers in parentheses that provide machine-parseable context. These complement — not replace — the inline commenting labels above.

ReviewLabel.name: security:
ReviewLabel.meaning: [NEW in v3.0] Security risk requiring immediate attention.

Decoration.name: if-minor
Decoration.meaning: Fix only if change is small.

Decoration.name: agent-safe
Decoration.meaning: [NEW in v3.0] Safe for AI agent auto-fix.

Decoration.name: agent-skip
Decoration.meaning: [NEW in v3.0] Do NOT delegate to AI agent.

DocCommentStandards.Description: Public API surfaces — classes, interfaces, public methods — MUST carry machine-readable documentation comments. Inline labels (above) annotate implementation logic; doc-comment blocks annotate contracts consumed by tooling, IDEs, and generated documentation.

Standard.Example: /** * Calculates the arithmetic mean of two operands. * * @param x - First input number. * @param y - Second input number. * @returns The arithmetic mean of `x` and `y`. * @throws {@link RangeError} if either operand is NaN. * * @example * ```ts * getAverage(4, 6); // returns 5 * ``` */ const getAverage = (x: number, y: number): number => (x + y) / 2;

Standard.OptionalTags: remarks example seealso value typeparam inheritdoc

Standard.Example:
def process_payment(order: Order) -> PaymentReceipt: """Process payment for a confirmed order.
Args: order: The order entity to charge. Must have a positive total.
Returns: PaymentReceipt containing the gateway transaction ID.
Raises: PaymentTimeoutException: Gateway did not respond in 30 s. InsufficientFundsException: Payment method was declined. """

Standard.Note: Rustdoc comments use Markdown. The # Errors section is required for functions returning Result. # Safety is required for unsafe functions. Doctests in # Examples are compiled and run by cargo test.

Standard.RequiredTags: Function summary (first sentence), param/return in prose
Standard.Note: GoDoc extracts the first sentence of a comment as the summary. There are no structured tags — document parameters and return values in prose. Deprecated items use "Deprecated:" as the first word.

AntiPattern.name: Redundancy
AntiPattern.Description: Comment restates what the code already says.
AntiPattern.Bad: // Assign: Set order ID to 123 order.Id = 123;
AntiPattern.Good: // Assign: Order ID from payment gateway response — gateway is source of truth order.Id = paymentResponse.OrderId;

AntiPattern.name: Vagueness
AntiPattern.Description: Label is present but subject gives no useful information.
AntiPattern.Good: // Validate: Order meets minimum purchase and in-stock requirements before payment

AntiPattern.name: Over-commenting
AntiPattern.Description: Every trivial line carries a comment, drowning signal in noise.
AntiPattern.Good: // Create: Cart pre-populated with customer's saved items for one-click checkout var items = new List<Item>(customer.SavedItems);

AntiPattern.name: Inconsistent style
AntiPattern.Description: Mixed capitalisation and labelling breaks grep-ability and scanning.

AntiPattern.name: Stale comments
AntiPattern.Description: Comment describes old behaviour that the code has since evolved beyond.

AntiPattern.name: Commented-out code
AntiPattern.Description: Dead code left commented-out pollutes the file. Use version control (git) instead.

AntiPattern.name: Verbose agent context
AntiPattern.Description: [NEW in v3.0] Bloated CAT-10 annotations that attempt to fully describe the codebase in comments. An ETH Zurich study (AGENTbench, 2026) shows that verbose LLM-generated context reduces agent task success rates by ~3% and increases inference costs by 20%. Keep agent annotations concise and factual — one constraint per line.
AntiPattern.Good: // AgentHint: do NOT add DB calls here — use the repository injected in the ctor; // validation lives in OrderValidator, not here

AntiPattern.name: Passive voice in comment body
AntiPattern.Description: [NEW in v3.0] Passive voice obscures the agent or intent. Use imperative-mood verbs.
AntiPattern.Bad: // Filter: Expired sessions are removed from the cache
AntiPattern.Good: // Filter: Remove expired sessions from cache to prevent stale auth

BestPractices.Practice: Comment the WHY, never the WHAT.
Capitalise first word after the colon.
Align comment with its code block's indentation.
Max 100 characters per comment line (80 for legacy).
Use comments sparingly — naming and structure first.
Write the comment while writing the code — never retroactively.
Use IDE-standard tags (TSDoc / XML-doc / GoDoc) for all public API surfaces.
Establish a team commenting vocabulary and enforce it in code review.
Prefer verbs over nouns: "Filter expired sessions" not "Expired session filter".
[NEW] Apply the Semantic Density Principle: every token in a comment must earn its place. Remove filler words.
[NEW] Prefer CAT-10 annotations for agent-consumed boundaries; keep them human-curated, not LLM-generated.
[NEW] When code will be edited by AI agents, add AgentHint: and Boundary: labels at decision points.
[NEW] Attribution: link to external specs, ADRs, or tickets using Context: rather than embedding URLs in arbitrary comments.

ContextGuidelines.Context: Use Enforce: and Validate: liberally to make domain policies explicit and searchable. Add Policy: references to compliance frameworks.
Always pair Call:, Send:, and Receive: comments with the system name and the data contract version where possible.
Use Cache:, Compute:, and Profile: to flag hotspots. Include the measured or expected order of magnitude. Add PERF marker for known issues.
Bracket with Guard:, Catch:, and Compensate: to make failure modes explicit for future maintainers.
Use Await:, Lock:, and Throttle: consistently so that concurrency boundaries are immediately visible on scan. Add Circuit: for resilience patterns.
Always comment validation logic with Validate: or Guard: plus the threat being mitigated (e.g., "SQL injection", "SSRF", "replay attack").
[NEW in v3.0] Add Contract:, Invariant:, and Boundary: at module entry points. Use AgentSkip: for hand-tuned sections. Use AgentHint: at complex branching points. Keep annotations concise — see AP-7.
[NEW in v3.0] Use BREAKING temporal marker on any public surface change. All public APIs require doc-comment coverage (BP-10). Mark internal helpers with @internal / internal visibility modifiers.

Phase.name: Foundation
Phase.Task: Agree on team commenting vocabulary and add to style guide.
Create IDE snippets for the most common labels (Validate, Guard, Catch, Call, Log).
Add label consistency check to code-review checklist.
Apply to all new code and critical business-logic paths first.
[NEW] Identify code paths regularly edited by AI agents and add Contract: + Boundary: annotations.

Phase.name: Adoption
Phase.Task: Apply during routine refactoring — no big-bang rewrites.
